issues.legal_issue: A judicial or quasi-judicial authority cannot review its earlier order without a power of review granted by law, and a court cannot confer that power.
material_facts: The Corporation had earlier approved the hoarding after an administrative examination.
The High Court permitted the Corporation to withdraw its earlier approval and pass a fresh order, although no power of review had been identified.
The Corporation then passed a fresh order that did not approve the hoarding.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not confer review jurisdiction on the Corporation. Its order permitting review was without jurisdiction and a nullity, and the consequential order passed by the Corporation was unenforceable.
issues.legal_principle: Review is not an inherent power and must be expressly or impliedly conferred by law; an order reviewing an earlier order without that power is without jurisdiction. The Court relied on Patel Chunibhai Dajibha v. Narayanrao Khanderao Jambekar, AIR 1965 SC 1457; Harbhajan Singh v. Karam Singh, AIR 1966 SC 641; Patel Narshi Thakershi v. Shri Pradyuman Singhji Arjunsinghji, AIR 1970 SC 1273; Maj. Chandra Bhan Singh v. Latafat Ullah Khan, AIR 1978 SC 1814; Dr. Smt. Kuntesh Gupta v. Management of Hindu Kanya Mahavidhyalaya, AIR 1987 SC 2186; State of Orissa v. Commissioner of Land Records and Settlement, (1998) 7 SCC 162; and Sunita Jain v. Pawan Kumar Jain, (2008) 2 SCC 705.

predicates.review_of_quasi_judicial_order: An authority reconsidered and altered its own earlier judicial or quasi-judicial order.
predicates.no_review_power_granted_by_law: The law did not grant the authority power to review its earlier order.

issues.definition: When an authority reviews an earlier judicial or quasi-judicial order without power granted by law, the review order is without jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot retain the benefit of interim or consequential orders after voluntarily withdrawing the proceeding in which those orders were obtained.
material_facts: The petitioners obtained interim orders in a writ petition and consequential orders were passed by the Corporation pursuant to them.
The petitioners then voluntarily withdrew the writ petition after stating that their grievance had been redressed.
The appellant sought to prevent the withdrawn petition's orders from continuing to affect its agreement with the Society.
issues.conclusion: The orders made in the withdrawn writ petition and the consequential orders made pursuant to them stood washed away, and the petitioners could not claim their continuing benefit. The parties could proceed with their agreement as if those orders had not adversely affected it, subject to orders made independently of the withdrawn proceeding.
issues.legal_principle: Interim orders merge into the final disposition and do not survive dismissal or withdrawal of the proceeding; restitution requires that an advantage obtained through an interim order be neutralized when the proceeding ends without a merits determination supporting that advantage. The Court relied on Dr. A.R. Sircar v. State of Uttar Pradesh, 1993 Supp. (2) SCC 734; Shiv Shanker v. Board of Directors, Uttar Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation, 1995 Supp. (2) SCC 726; Committee of Management, Arya Inter College v. Sree Kumar Tiwary, AIR 1997 SC 3071; GTC Industries Ltd. v. Union of India, AIR 1998 SC 1566; Jaipur Municipal Corporation v. C.L. Mishra, (2005) 8 SCC 423; Ram Krishna Verma v. State of U.P., AIR 1992 SC 1888; Grindlays Bank Ltd. v. Income Tax Officer, AIR 1980 SC 656; South Eastern Coalfields Ltd. v. State of M.P., AIR 2003 SC 4482; Karnataka Rare Earth v. Senior Geologist, (2004) 2 SCC 783; Badrinath v. State of Tamil Nadu, AIR 2000 SC 3243; and Abhimanyoo Ram v. State of U.P., (2008) 17 SCC 73.

predicates.writ_petition_withdrawn_after_interim_re: A party voluntarily withdrew a writ petition after obtaining interim relief in it.
predicates.consequential_orders_based_on_interim_re: Other orders were made as a consequence of the interim relief granted in that proceeding.

issues.definition: When a party withdraws a writ petition after obtaining interim relief and consequential orders were made on its basis, those orders are neutralized.

issues.legal_issue: An administrative order changing an earlier decision is vitiated when affected parties are denied a hearing and the authority gives no reasons for the change.
material_facts: The Corporation changed its earlier approval and issued a fresh order not approving the hoarding.
The appellant and the Society were not given an opportunity to be heard before the fresh order was made.
The Corporation gave no reasons or explanation of the material on which it based the change.
issues.conclusion: The Corporation's fresh order was vitiated for denying a hearing and failing to record reasons; those circumstances established legal malice.
issues.legal_principle: Administrative action must be fair and comply with natural justice; an authority changing an earlier order must explain the material supporting the change. Legal malice means an act done wrongfully and wilfully without lawful excuse, including an exercise of power for a purpose foreign to that for which it is intended. The Court relied on Addl. Distt. Magistrate, Jabalpur v. Shivakant Shukla, AIR 1976 SC 1207; Smt. S.R. Venkataraman v. Union of India, AIR 1979 SC 49; State of A.P. v. Goverdhanlal Pitti, AIR 2003 SC 1941; Chairman and M.D., B.P.L. Ltd. v. S.P. Gururaja, (2003) 8 SCC 567; West Bengal State Electricity Board v. Dilip Kumar Ray, AIR 2007 SC 976; Punjab State Electricity Board Ltd. v. Zora Singh, (2005) 6 SCC 776; and Union of India v. V. Ramakrishnan, (2005) 8 SCC 394.

predicates.administrative_reconsideration_of_prior_: An administrative authority reconsidered and changed an earlier order.
predicates.affected_parties_denied_hearing: The authority did not give the affected parties an opportunity to be heard before changing the order.
predicates.reasons_not_given: The authority gave no reasons or explanation of the material supporting its changed decision.

issues.definition: When an administrative authority changes an earlier order without hearing the affected parties or giving reasons, the changed order is vitiated and legally malicious.
